extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, legislators, students of political economy, and informed readers interested in trade policy
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for judging when and how to restrict or encourage foreign trade (monopolies, duties, navigation acts, retaliation, and restoring free trade), aimed at guiding policy decisions about protectionism and commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow individuals to choose how to employ their capital
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the species of domestic industry which his capital can employ, and of which the produce is likely to be of the greatest value, every individual, it is evident, can in his local situation judge much better than any statesman or lawgiver can do for him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A statesman attempting to direct private people in employing capital would assume an authority safe for no person or council; local knowledge lets individuals allocate capital more productively than centralized direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not give the home market a domestic monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: To give the monopoly of the home market to the produce of domestic industry ... is in some measure to direct private people in what manner they ought to employ their capitals, and must in almost all cases be either a useless or a hurtful regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If domestic produce can be brought as cheap as foreign, the regulation is useless; if it cannot, it is generally hurtful. Example: household prudence—tailor buys shoes rather than makes them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialize and buy when foreigners supply more cheaply
rubrics_metrics.description: If a foreign country can supply us with a commodity cheaper than we ourselves can make it, better buy it of them with some part of the produce of our own industry, employed in a way in which we have some advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative advantage: national industry should be left to find its most advantageous employments; buying cheaper imports preserves or increases the exchangeable value of annual produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection rarely increases total industry or revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Though ... a particular manufacture may sometimes be acquired sooner than it could have been otherwise, ... it will by no means follow that the sum-total, either of its industry, or of its revenue, can ever be augmented by any such regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry and capital grow only as capital is saved out of revenue; immediate protective regulations typically diminish revenue and therefore are unlikely to accelerate capital accumulation overall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer buying from countries with natural or acquired advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the advantages which one country has over another, in producing particular commodities, be natural or acquired, is in this respect of no consequence. As long as the one country has those advantages ... it will always be more advantageous for the latter rather to buy of the former than to make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: trying to grow grapes/wine in Scotland at enormous expense is unreasonable compared to importing from climates with natural advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider transportation and bulk when assessing import competition
rubrics_metrics.description: The freest importation of foreign cattle, for example, were made ever so free, so few could be imported, that the grazing trade of Great Britain could be little affected... Corn is a much more bulky commodity than butcher’s meat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bulky or hard-to-transport goods (live cattle, grain) are less likely to undercut domestic producers; fine manufactures are more easily transported and more vulnerable to foreign competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufactures are more exposed to foreign competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufactures, those of the finer kind especially, are more easily transported from one country to another than corn or cattle. In manufactures, a very small advantage will enable foreigners to undersell our own workmen, even in the home market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy should recognize that some industries (silks, linen) are more likely to suffer from trade liberalization than bulky agricultural goods; exporters who can compete abroad will generally retain home markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit protection to cases necessary for national defence
rubrics_metrics.description: The first is, when some particular sort of industry is necessary for the defence of the country. The defence of Great Britain ... depends very much upon the number of its sailors and shipping. The act of navigation ... endeavours to give the sailors and shipping of Great Britain the monopoly of the trade of their own country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defence-critical industries (shipping, sailors) justify trade restrictions or burdens because security can be prioritized over opulence; specific statutory dispositions (e.g., Navigation Acts) are examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equalize foreign imports where domestic goods bear a tax
rubrics_metrics.description: When some tax is imposed at home upon the produce of the latter, it seems reasonable that an equal tax should be imposed upon the like produce of the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imposing an equivalent duty on imports simply levels the competition distorted by domestic taxation; this prevents tax-driven diversion of capital into less natural employments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retaliation only when likely to secure repeal of foreign barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be good policy in retaliations of this kind, when there is a probability that they will procure the repeal of the high duties or prohibitions complained of. ... When there is no probability that any such repeal can be procured, it seems a bad method ... to do another injury ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retaliatory duties/prohibitions are justified as leverage to obtain foreign market access; absent plausible leverage, retaliation imposes broad costs domestically and is unwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid broad retaliations that tax the entire country for narrow gains
rubrics_metrics.description: When our neighbours prohibit some manufacture of ours, we generally prohibit, not only the same, for that alone would seldom affect them considerably, but some other manufacture of theirs... Every such law, therefore, imposes a real tax upon the whole country, not in favour of that particular class of workmen ... but of some other class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retaliation often protects different domestic producers than those harmed abroad, while imposing costs on almost all citizens; policymakers should beware of such hidden taxation effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore free trade gradually when many depend on protected industries
rubrics_metrics.description: Humanity may in this case require that the freedom of trade should be restored only by slow gradations, and with a good deal of reserve and circumspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gradual removal may mitigate transitional unemployment of many thousands; however, author argues actual disruption is often smaller because exported manufactures keep markets and workers can shift occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect limited disruption when restoring freedom: exported manufactures persist
rubrics_metrics.description: All those manufactures of which any part is commonly exported to other European countries without a bounty, could be very little affected by the freest importation of foreign goods. Such manufactures ... would still keep possession of the home market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufactures successfully exported abroad tend to be price-competitive and will retain home markets under liberalization; fashion-driven preference for foreign wares affects only a small segment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour mobility cushions adjustment to trade liberalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Though a great number of people should ... be thrown all at once out of their ordinary employment ... it would by no means follow that they would thereby be deprived either of employment or subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: demobilized soldiers/seamen largely found other employment; manufacturers' habits make them more adaptable than soldiers; collateral industries allow transfer of workmen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes on necessaries complicate fair adjustment of import duties
rubrics_metrics.description: It might always be known with great exactness, how far the price of such a commodity could be enhanced by such a tax; but how far the general enhancement of the price of labour might affect that of every different commodity ... could never be known with any tolerable exactness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When necessaries are taxed, it's hard to proportion foreign duties to offset complex general price and labour-cost effects; heavy taxes on necessities act like poor soil/climate and industry should be left to adapt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetual prohibitions on imports limit population and industry
rubrics_metrics.description: To prohibit, by a perpetual law, the importation of foreign corn and cattle, is in reality to enact, that the population and industry of the country shall, at no time, exceed what the rude produce of its own soil can maintain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term import bans effectively cap growth by tying population and productive capacity to domestic agricultural limits; this is a serious cost of permanent protection.
